BACK TO PORTFOLIO

Executive Summary & Overview

This engagement involved a deep dive into suspicious outbound network connections originating from an internal system within WayneCorpInc. The organization, which explicitly does not utilize Amazon Web Services, detected communications with multiple EC2 instances. The primary objective was to conduct a thorough investigation using Splunk and Sysmon logs to understand the scope of the compromise, identify the source of the activity, and gather indicators for incident response and threat intelligence sharing.

The investigation successfully identified a compromised web server, we1149srv.waynecorpinc.local, from which a malicious executable, C:\inetpub\wwwroot\joomla\3791.exe, was initiating connections to AWS infrastructure. Analysis revealed the initial access vector involved a file upload via a POST request to /joomla/administrator/index.php, originating from an external IP address. The executable's SHA256 hash was used for online reputation checks, revealing additional associated malicious IPs. This writeup details the steps taken to uncover the incident, from initial detection to identifying the full attack chain.

To start Splunk, open a terminal and run the command sudo systemctl start Splunkd then open Firefox and navigate to 127.0.0.1:8000. All Splunk searches were performed with index=* and a timeframe of 'All Time'.

Asset Information

HOSTNAME SUMMARY
we1149srv.waynecorpinc.local Windows Server (IP: 192.168.250.70) identified as the source of suspicious outbound connections to AWS EC2 instances. A malicious executable, C:\inetpub\wwwroot\joomla\3791.exe, was found in its web root, responsible for the unauthorized communications.

Question & Answer Solutions

1. WayneCorpInc doesn't use Amazon Web Service for cloud hosting, so when a threat hunting discovered outbound connections to EC2 instances they immediately began to drilldown into this activity so they can provide as much context for the Incident Response Team as possible. Using Sysmon logs, how many destination hostnames are found? (Format: # Destination EC2s)

3

Reasoning: A Splunk search for index=* ec2 revealed events related to EC2 instances. Further refinement using | rex field=_raw "\"rdata\":\"(?<ec2_instance>ec2-[^\"]+amazonaws\.com)\"" | stats dc(ec2_instance) confirmed 3 unique destination EC2 hostnames.

2. Enter the hostnames (excluding '.compute-1.amazon.aws.com') in the order of event count, with the highest first (Format: Hostname1, Hostname2, ...)

ec2-23-22-63-114, ec2-184-72-234-184, ec2-52-70-175-181

Reasoning: Using the search index=* | rex field=_raw "\"rdata\":\"(?<ec2_instance>ec2-[^\"]+amazonaws\.com)\"" | where isnotnull(ec2_instance) | stats count by ec2_instance | sort -count, the unique EC2 hostnames were extracted, counted, and sorted by their event frequency.

3. Look at the Image 'interesting field' to see what files are initiating these connections. What is the Image value with the lowest count? (Format: Image Value)

C:\inetpub\wwwroot\joomla\3791.exe

Reasoning: By searching for index=* EventCode=3 | stats count by Image | sort count, we identified the executable paths responsible for network connections and sorted them to find the one with the lowest event count.

4. What is the hostname and internal IP address of the system that initiated this connection? (Format: Hostname, X.X.X.X)

we1149srv.waynecorpinc.local, 192.168.250.70

Reasoning: Filtering for index=* Image="C:\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\joomla\\3791.exe" EventCode=3 revealed the source hostname (ComputerName) and internal IP address (SourceIp) of the system initiating the connections.

5. What time was this connection event? Use TimeCreated SystemTime (Format: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS)

2016-08-10T21:56:19

Reasoning: By examining the specific Sysmon EventCode=3 log for the identified executable and source system, the TimeCreated SystemTime field provided the exact timestamp.

6. What is the destination hostname and IP address of the AWS EC2 instance? (Format: Hostname, X.X.X.X)

ec2-23-22-63-114.compute-1.amazonaws.com, 23.22.63.114

Reasoning: Within the same Sysmon EventCode=3 log, the DestinationHostname and DestinationIp fields provided the required information.

7. Utilize Sysmon logs to find the SHA256 hash of the executable making this connection. What is the hash value? (Format: SHA256 Hash)

EC78C938D8453739CA2A370B9C275971EC46CAF6E479DE2B2D04E97CC47FA45D

Reasoning: A Splunk search for index=* Image="C:\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\joomla\\3791.exe" EventCode=1 (process creation) allowed us to locate the Hashes field, which contained the SHA256 hash of the executable.

8. Search this hash online to find more about its reputation. On the Behaviour tab look at the results for Microsoft Sysinternals. What two IPv4 addresses are listed, that begin with 23.216.? (Format: X.X.X.X, X.X.X.X)

23.216.147.64, 23.216.147.76

Reasoning: The SHA256 hash was submitted to VirusTotal. Under the "Behaviour" tab, within the Microsoft Sysinternals analysis, two IPv4 addresses starting with 23.216. were identified.

9. Using these two gathered IPs, check to see if there is any activity from them in Splunk, which there might not be! What is the number of events per IP where the address is mentioned ANYWHERE in a log? (Format: IP1EventCount, IP2EventCount)

0, 0

Reasoning: A Splunk search for index=* 23.216.147.64 OR 23.216.147.76 across all raw logs yielded no results, indicating no internal activity related to these specific IPs.

10. At what time was this file uploaded to the web server? (Use 'timestamp' value) (Format: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS)

2016-08-10T15:52:45

Reasoning: By searching for events related to 3791.exe and sorting by time, specifically looking at web server access logs, the timestamp of the file upload was identified.

11. What user-agent was used to upload the file? (Format: Full User-Agent)

Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko

Reasoning: In the same web server access log entry as the file upload, the http.http_user_agent field contained the full user-agent string used by the attacker.

12. What URI received a POST request from the attacker, in order to upload the file? (Format: /path/to/something)

/joomla/administrator/index.php

Reasoning: The web server access logs for the file upload event clearly showed the URI that received the POST request.

13. What is the source IP responsible for the initial access activity? (Format: X.X.X.X)

40.80.148.42

Reasoning: The web server access log entry for the file upload also contained the SourceIp of the attacker.

14. We need to understand if any of our network defenses have detected this activity, or if we're completely blind. Use one of the retrieved indicators to search the logs to see if anything has flagged this file as being malicious. Provide any timestamp retrieved from a relevant log to show evidence of some kind of alert or notification (Format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS)

2016-08-10 15:52:45

Reasoning: Searching for index=* "http.http_user_agent"="Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko" alert revealed an alert log entry with the specified timestamp, indicating detection of the malicious user-agent.

Key Takeaways & Security Insights

  • •
    Unusual Outbound Connections: Unsanctioned outbound connections to cloud providers like Amazon Web Services EC2 instances are critical indicators of compromise, especially in environments where such services are not authorized.
  • •
    Endpoint Visibility with Sysmon: Sysmon EventCode 3 (Network Connection) is invaluable for identifying the originating process (Image), source IP, and destination details of suspicious network activity.
  • •
    Web Server Compromise: The presence of a malicious executable (3791.exe) in a public web root directory (C:\inetpub\wwwroot\joomla\) strongly suggests a web application vulnerability (e.g., Joomla) leading to arbitrary file upload.
  • •
    Threat Intelligence Integration: Leveraging SHA256 hashes for online reputation checks (e.g., VirusTotal) is crucial for confirming maliciousness and discovering associated indicators like additional C2 infrastructure.
  • •
    User-Agent and URI Analysis: Malicious User-Agents combined with unauthorized POST requests to sensitive URIs (e.g., /joomla/administrator/index.php) are strong indicators of initial access and compromise.
  • •
    Centralized Logging with Splunk: Splunk facilitates the correlation of diverse log sources (Sysmon, web server access logs) to reconstruct attack timelines, identify initial vectors, and track post-exploitation activities.
  • •
    Proactive Alerting: The detection of an alert based on the malicious User-Agent underscores the importance of robust network defenses and SIEM rules configured to flag known bad indicators, enabling timely incident response.
